summary: Documents usage patterns and issues when deploying a home network for NEMO-enabled mobile routers conforming to NEMO Basic Support. It gives examples of how a home network can be organized, drawn from discussions on NEMO mailing lists. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A traveling network has a home base it comes back to. This note shows different ways that home base can be arranged.

questions: what is a nemo home network
how to deploy a nemo home network
subtitle: Different ways to organize the home network for mobile routers that travel with their networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile routers that carry entire networks with them (like a traveling company network) need a place to come home to, but NEMO Basic Support allows for different ways to organize that home network depending on deployment needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents five models for home network organization: traditional Mobile IPv6 home networks, extended networks that append mobile network prefixes, aggregated networks where mobile networks overlap the home, virtual networks with no physical home link, and hierarchical networks where mobile routers act as home agents for their own networks.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can choose the home network model that best matches their mobile router deployment, from simple single-router networks to complex hierarchies supporting nested mobile networks.

today: RFC 4887 is an Informational RFC that documents usage patterns for NEMO. It does not define protocols but instead provides guidance for network operators deploying mobile routers with networks. The framework remains applicable to modern mobile and edge networks where groups of devices move together while maintaining connectivity.

sections.title: Mobile Networks and Home Networks
sections.content:
RFC 4887 documents how to organize home networks for Network Mobility (NEMO)-enabled mobile routers. In NEMO, a mobile router moves around but carries one or more networks with it (called Mobile Networks). This is different from Mobile IPv6, which only handles individual mobile nodes. The RFC assumes familiarity with IPv6 mobility and NEMO Basic Support, and documents practical deployment models based on discussions in the NEMO community.

A key insight is that the home network can encompass more than just a home link; it includes the home link and all the networks that mobile routers carry with them. The document presents five different ways to organize this home network. Each model represents a different tradeoff between simplicity and capability, depending on whether the mobile routers have multiple tiers, whether a physical home link exists, and how network prefixes are managed.
sections.eli5: When a traveling network comes home, it needs to connect to a home base. But how that connection works depends on how the home and the traveling network are organized.

sections.title: NEMO Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC builds on terminology from Mobile IPv6 and NEMO specifications. Key terms include the Home Link, the physical subnet at the home agent location; the Mobile Network Prefix (MNP), the IPv6 address space carried by a mobile router; and the Home Address, an address a mobile node or mobile router uses to identify itself. When a mobile router comes home, it may use a home address from the home link itself or from one of its mobile networks.

The document introduces additional terms specific to the different models: Extended Home Network where mobile networks are contiguous with a home link; Aggregated Home Network where mobile networks overlap with home space; Virtual Home Network where there is no physical home link; and Mobile Home Network which is hierarchical, with one home agent serving multiple mobile routers that themselves serve as home agents. In all cases, the aggregation of mobile networks is kept within the home agents and mobile routers; it is not advertised to the broader infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Each traveling network has a home address and a home base. The home can be organized in different ways depending on what the traveling networks need to do.

sections.title: NEMO Extended and Aggregated Home Networks
sections.content:
The NEMO Extended Home Network is the simplest model. It uses one global routing prefix (say /48) that is subdivided into subnets: one subnet for the home link (a /64) and other subnets for the mobile networks (each a /64). When a mobile router is at home, it performs normal routing between the home link and the mobile networks. When away, it registers with its home agent. This model trivially extends the Mobile IPv6 home network concept by adding prefixes for the mobile networks.

The NEMO Aggregated Home Network overlaps the mobile networks with the home link space. The mobile networks' prefixes are subnets of the same aggregation used for the home link. When at home, the mobile router acts as a bridge rather than a router. The home agent can route either way, and the mobile router can register using a home address from the home link or from one of its mobile networks. This model is more efficient in address space but more complex in routing logic.

Both models have deployment considerations: the mobile router must know how to transition from being at home to being away, and the home agent must be configured to handle the mobile routers' prefixes. Choice between these models depends on address space availability and whether administrators prefer routing or bridging at home.
sections.eli5: The simple way is to give the traveling network its own address space next to the home link. A fancier way is to make the traveling network part of the home address space.

sections.title: Virtual and Hierarchical Home Networks
sections.content:
The Virtual Home Network model has no physical home link at all. Instead, the home network exists as a virtual aggregation. The home agent advertises the aggregation to the infrastructure without advertising internal subnets. This is useful when there is no natural "home" location or when the home is purely logical. Mobile routers register with the home agent but do not have a physical home link to return to. The home agent maintains routing information internally for the subnets belonging to different mobile routers.

The NEMO Mobile Home Network model is hierarchical. A top-level home agent advertises one global aggregation prefix (e.g., /48). Underneath, mobile routers register their mobile network prefixes and act as home agents for their own sub-networks, creating multiple levels of aggregation. This enables scenarios like a traveling company network that itself has traveling sub-networks. Each tier of mobile router registers with the tier above it, creating a hierarchy where subnetting is kept internal and only the top aggregation is advertised externally.

These complex models are useful for large, structured mobile networks and multi-tier mobility scenarios, but require careful configuration and testing to ensure proper routing and address delegation at each level.
sections.eli5: Instead of a physical home, the traveling network can have a virtual home that exists only in the home agent's memory. And one traveling network can have its own traveling sub-networks underneath it, like a tree of networks.

sections.title: Applicability and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Each model is applicable to different scenarios. The Extended Home Network is appropriate when the organization has address space and simple topology: all mobile routers reporting to a single home agent. It is the most straightforward to deploy and understand. The Aggregated Home Network works when address space is limited and overlapping prefix management is acceptable; it requires more sophisticated routing at the home agent. The Virtual Home Network is useful when there is no permanent home location or when home and mobile prefixes should be completely separate logically.

The Mobile Home Network hierarchy is applicable to large deployments with structured mobility: for instance, a global company with regional mobile networks, each with their own mobile sub-networks. However, each layer adds complexity. Configuration errors at any level affect all lower layers. Administrators must ensure that home agents at each tier properly register with their parent home agents and that the hierarchy of prefixes is correctly maintained.

The RFC notes that all models assume Mobile IPv6 and NEMO Basic Support. The examples illustrate the basic support but do not limit its scope; future deployments may use additional mechanisms. The choice of model should be made based on organizational structure, address space constraints, and operational complexity tolerance.
sections.eli5: Simple networks use simple home organization. Big networks with many layers can use hierarchical homes, but they need more careful planning.
